Issue #14221 in matplotlib/matplotlib
Title: `ax.set_prop_cycle` does not allow 'CN' colors
State: OPEN
Author: u55
Comments: 15
Body: Hi matplotlib developers,
I was surprised to discover that the cycler validation does not allow colors specified with 'CN' syntax.
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from cycler import cycler

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.set_prop_cycle(cycler(color=['C1', 'C0'])) # raises ValueError
# ax.set_prop_cycle(cycler(color=['tab:orange', 'tab:blue'])) # works fine
ax.plot(np.arange(9))
ax.plot(-np.arange(9))
plt.show()
If matplotlib can differentiate between {'C0', 'C1', 'C2', 'C3', 'C4', 'C5', 'C6', 'C7', 'C8', 'C9'} colors and {'b', 'g', 'r', 'c', 'm', 'y', 'k', 'w'} colors (case insensitive) anywhere else that a color is specified, then it seems to me that the cycler should be able to handle this as well. Thanks.
Tested with matplotlib 3.0.3 and python 3.7.3 (Anaconda) on Windows 10.
Comments:
[1] That cannot be done reliably. 'CN' indexes into the default property cycle at execution time, which then just might be the cycler you created. Therefore cyclers themselves do not accept 'CN'.
[2] @timhoffm Thanks for the comment, but I don't fully understand. Are you saying it is a recursion issue? Why can't the cycler evaluate its input arguments at instantiation using the "currently defined" cycler, then use those values to create the "new" cycler?
[3] Cyclers don't do anything at instantiation time. Actually, it's not even the cycler that resolves the color. The color is resolved in the respective plotting function when it's called. If you want to use the colors of the existing cycler to create a new one, you'll have to get it's colors explicitly via cycler.by_key()['color'].
[4] There is some confusing naming here as rcparams_setup has a cycler function which wraps cycler.cycler and we import various places.
In Axes.set_prop_cycle we are re-using the validation code that we use when parsing rcparams from file (which as part of start up, is clearly not going to work as we are loading the cycle to be the default cycle).
It would certainly be possible to special case the color key in Axes.set_prop_cycle, before we validate, but I am not sure it is worth it.  @u55 What is the use-case for this ?
You can currently get this to work via
import matplotlib.colors as mcolors
ax.set_prop_cycle(cycler(color=mcolors.to_rgba_array(['C1', 'C0'])))
which does the look up against the default color cycle before you pass it in.
[5] @tacaswell Indeed, my use-case is simply that it is easier for me to remember, and faster to type:
ax.set_prop_cycle(cycler(color=['C1', 'C0']))
than:
import matplotlib.colors as mcolors
ax.set_prop_cycle(cycler(color=mcolors.to_rgba_array(['C1', 'C0'])))
which seems like a hackish work-around.
Furthermore, as an end user, it seems inconsistent and unexpected that every other color specification (i.e. 'tab:blue', 'xkcd:sky blue', 'b', '#0000FF', 'blue', (0, 0, 1), '0.5', etc.) works fine with the prop_cycle but 'C0', etc., fails. It sounds like you are saying that the validation for Axes.set_prop_cycle is over-zealous. If so, then why not fix it?
Also, I don't understand the validation for parsing rcParams. The axes.prop_cycle entry in my '.matplotlibrc' file is commented out, which means the actual default values must be hard-coded somewhere. Why can't 'CN' index into this default color cycle?
[6] Given the discussion at #12967 I think eagerly resolving colors (against whatever the previous color cycle (the default one if there's none yet, e.g. in the matplotlibrc) is) makes sense here?
[7] Probably yes. But I really recommend not to add this additional functionality until we've determined and implemented a clear global resolution strategy - when and from which cycler. Otherwise this implementation might not match the desired behavior.
[8] Updated the issue title to be a bit clearer about where the validation is being done.
@timhoffm @anntzer Seems reasonable to move to eager color evaluation. This also would also move us a long way towards "always store colors and RBGA float tuples internally".  On the other hand, this would mean that a.set_color(C); C != a.get_color() in general which is not great.  Not sure carrying 2 copies of the color (one 'human readable', one 'RGBA') is a better path though.
Currently, we have to resolve CN against the default cycle from rcparams because the Axes does not actually hold the underlying cycler instance, it only holds an itertools.cycle() of the cycler.  Even though it cuts off some use-cases (like having 4 axes each with their own property cycler that have different colors and then expecting 'C0' to have different values in each), it greatly simplifies both implementation and how hard it is to explain to always go against the default cycle .
[9] What about making a Color class? We could internally use this and return it for get_color(). That would allow Color('r') == 'red' so that get_color() == 'r', get_color() == 'red', get_color() == (1, 0, 0) all would work.
Of course, this is a breaking API change, however AFAIC we're not consistent here anyway. E.g. Rectangle.set_facecolor currently normalizes to RGBA, but Text.set_color just keeps it as is.
In [12]: from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle                                                                     
In [13]: r = Rectangle((0, 0), 1,1)                                                                                   

In [16]: r.get_facecolor()                                                                                            
Out[16]: (0.12156862745098039, 0.4666666666666667, 0.7058823529411765, 1.0)

In [17]: r.set_color('b')                                                                                             

In [18]: r.get_facecolor()                                                                                            
Out[18]: (0.0, 0.0, 1.0, 1)

and
In [19]: from matplotlib.text import Text                                          
[10] We could make Color inherit from tuple, but just override __eq__ so that it converts the other argument with to_color_rgba first before comparing (possibly, also stash the arguments with which it was constructed and use it in its __str__/__repr__ as well).
So something very approximately like
class Color(tuple):
    def __new__(cls, *args, **kwargs):
        self = cls(*mcolors.to_rgba(*args, **kwargs))
        self._args, self._kwargs = args, kwargs
        return self
    def __eq__(self, other):
        return tuple(self) == mcolors.to_rgba(other)
    def __str__(self):
        return super().__str__(self) + f" (a.k.a. Color(*{self._args}, **{self._kwargs}))"

[12] @angelazb no one is working on this, however from reviewing the discussion there is not a consensus of the direction we want to do.  What aspect of this do you want to work on?

Issue #25345 in matplotlib/matplotlib
Title: [Bug]: using clf and pyplot.draw in range slider on_changed callback blocks input to widgets
State: CLOSED
Author: schneichr
Comments: 13
Body: Bug summary
When using clear figure, adding new widgets and then redrawing the current figure in the on_changed callback of a range slider the inputs to all the widgets in the figure are blocked. When doing the same in the button callback on_clicked, everything works fine.
Code for reproduction
import matplotlib.pyplot as pyplot
import matplotlib.widgets as widgets

def onchanged(values):
    print("on changed")
    print(values)
    pyplot.clf()
    addElements()
    pyplot.draw()

def onclick(e):
    print("on click")
    pyplot.clf()
    addElements()
    pyplot.draw()

def addElements():
    ax = pyplot.axes([0.1, 0.45, 0.8, 0.1])
    global slider
    slider = widgets.RangeSlider(ax, "Test", valmin=1, valmax=10, valinit=(1, 10))
    slider.on_changed(onchanged)
    ax = pyplot.axes([0.1, 0.30, 0.8, 0.1])
    global button
    button = widgets.Button(ax, "Test")
    button.on_clicked(onclick)

addElements()

pyplot.show()
Actual outcome
The widgets can't receive any input from a mouse click, when redrawing in the on_changed callback of a range Slider.
When using a button, there is no problem.
Expected outcome
The range slider callback on_changed behaves the same as the button callback on_clicked.
Additional information
The problem also occurred on Manjaro with:

Python version: 3.10.9
Matplotlib version: 3.6.2
Matplotlib backend: QtAgg
Installation of matplotlib via Linux package manager

Operating system
Windows 10
Matplotlib Version
3.6.2
Matplotlib Backend
TkAgg
Python version
3.11.0
Jupyter version
No response
Installation
pip
Comments:
[1] A can confirm this behavior, but removing and recreating the objects that host the callbacks in the callbacks is definitely on the edge of the intended usage.
Why are you doing this?  In your application can you get away with not destroying your slider?
[2] I think there could be a way to not destroy the slider. But I don't have the time to test that currently.
My workaround for the problem was using a button to redraw everything. With that everything is working fine.
That was the weird part for me as they are both callbacks, but in one everything works fine and in the other one all inputs are blocked. If what I'm trying doing is not the intended usage, that's fine for me.
Thanks for the answer.
[3] The idiomatic way to destructively work on widgets that triggered an event in a UI toolkit is to do the destructive work in an idle callback:
def redraw():
    pyplot.clf()
    addElements()
    pyplot.draw()
    return False

def onchanged(values):
    print("on changed")
    print(values)
    pyplot.gcf().canvas.new_timer(redraw)
[4] Thanks for the answer. I tried that with the code in the original post.
The line:
pyplot.gcf().canvas.new_timer(redraw)
doesn't work for me. After having a look at the documentation, I think the line should be:
pyplot.gcf().canvas.new_timer(callbacks=[(redraw, tuple(), dict())])
But that still didn't work. The redraw callback doesn't seem to trigger.
[5] Sorry, I mean to update that after testing and before posting, but forgot to. That line should be:
    pyplot.gcf().canvas.new_timer(callbacks=[redraw])
[6] Sorry for double posting; now I see that it didn't actually get called!
That's because I forgot to call start as well, and the timer was garbage collected at the end of the function. It should be called as you've said, but stored globally and started:
import matplotlib.pyplot as pyplot
import matplotlib.widgets as widgets


def redraw():
    print("redraw")
    pyplot.clf()
    addElements()
    pyplot.draw()
    return False


def onchanged(values):
    print("on changed")
    print(values)
    global timer
    timer = pyplot.gcf().canvas.new_timer(callbacks=[(redraw, (), {})])
    timer.start()


def onclick(e):
    print("on click")
    global timer
    timer = pyplot.gcf().canvas.new_timer(callbacks=[(redraw, (), {})])
    timer.start()


def addElements():
    ax = pyplot.axes([0.1, 0.45, 0.8, 0.1])
    global slider
    slider = widgets.RangeSlider(ax, "Test", valmin=1, valmax=10, valinit=(1, 10))
    slider.on_changed(onchanged)

Title: [ENH]: Built-in crosshair tool through gui-native crosshair cursor
State: OPEN
Author: timhoffm
Comments: 13
Body: Problem
Our naive approaches to crosshair cursors https://matplotlib.org/devdocs/gallery/widgets/cursor.html have the disadvantage that the crosshair is drawn on the figure. This means an expensive redraw of the the figure for every cursor position change and results in a laggy behavior.
Proposed solution
We could grow an API on Canvas to draw a crosshair with GUI native lines. That should be relatively easy. We only need the size of the Axes-under-cursor in figure coordinates to determine the length of the crosshair.
The goal would be to add a crosshair tool in addtion to Pan and Zoom.
This tool should be much easier to use than a Cursor widget and much more efficient.
